system:
You are a computational cancer biologist searching CRISPR screen data for selective genetic dependencies: genes that cancer cells with a particular alteration (the biomarker) need more than other cancer cells do. Such genes are candidate drug targets with a built-in patient-selection strategy.

Work like a careful scientist:
1. Plan first with write_plan, and revise it as you learn.
2. Survey the data (genome_wide_top, scan_biomarker, scan_target) to generate candidate hypotheses.
3. Be sceptical before you believe a signal. Use inspect_association to check whether it is driven by one lineage or a disease subtype hiding inside a lineage, and whether the effect is large enough to matter. Ask whether the biology makes sense (paralog buffering, pathway dependence, oncogene addiction). A broadly essential target may lack a therapeutic window.
4. Literature search is not available in this session: judge novelty and mechanism from the data and your reasoning.
5. Register only your best hypotheses (register_hypothesis). Registration is final and must come before replication. You have 5 replications, each of which must pass one-sided p < 0.01 in BOTH held-out Broad cell lines and independent Sanger screens.
6. Report honestly with submit_findings. A hypothesis is replicated only if replicate() said so. Negative results are results. Never let what you remember from the literature override what the data show.

You have at most 15 model turns. Batch independent tool calls in one turn.
task_prompt:
Patient population of interest: cancers with biomarker LOSS_G13216 (loss of expression of gene G13216).

Find the single best candidate therapeutic target for this population: the gene these cell lines depend on most selectively, supported by the data. Register your top candidate (you may register up to two), replicate it, and submit findings with your best candidate listed first.

content.thinking:
G05992 is the strongest selective signal for LOSS_G13216, though it's broadly essential, so the selectivity is only a modest shift in mean fitness. Still, it's the best candidate here. I'm thinking the biomarker reflects a deletion or silencing of a gene, and I'm checking whether it shares a pattern with LOSS_G13741.

The gene's pattern points toward a co-deletion cluster with LOSS_G13741 and LOSS_G12910. I'm guessing G13216 loss makes the cell depend on G05992, perhaps through a paralog or pathway partner. I'll register G05992 with that synthetic-lethal mechanism, note that its novelty isn't found in the literature since I don't know the gene's identity, and then replicate.

Top-ranked pair in the genome-wide scan (beta -0.40, q ~1e-11), with the effect present within most lineages.

input.summary: Best candidate for LOSS_G13216 cancers is G05992. Loss of G13216 expression is associated with stronger dependence on G05992 in discovery lines (lineage-adjusted beta -0.40, q~1e-11; 99% of altered lines strongly dependent), and this replicated in held-out Broad lines (p=1e-8) and independent Sanger screens (p=2.5e-7). Caveats: G05992 is essential in most lines (about 485/495 unaltered lines also strongly dependent), so the window comes from a magnitude difference of roughly 0.4 Chronos units, not from absence of dependency in controls. The LOSS_G13216 signal also co-clusters with other losses (LOSS_G13741, LOSS_G12910), which may reflect shared chromosomal deletion, so a dosage-driven mechanism is possible. The other candidate, G05055, had a weaker and less selective signal (mean effect -0.19 vs -0.11, only 16/123 altered lines dependent) and was not registered. Mechanism is untested; I did not identify the genes by name in this session.
